chapters.title: Chapter 5: Valuation in Indian Corporate Practice

lessons.title: What Moves Your Company's Valuation: Decisions Managers Make Every Day

children.text: Valuation feels like something that happens to a company, decided by bankers in a conference room on one day of its life. It is not. The number is produced by decisions taken over years by people who never use the word valuation: the sales head who agrees 90 day credit to win an order, the plant manager who defers a machine replacement, the founder who never got round to separating personal expenses from the company's books. This lesson connects those decisions to the arithmetic.

body.text: You cannot negotiate your way to a higher valuation in the final month. You build it, or destroy it, through ordinary operating decisions over the two or three years before anybody opens a spreadsheet.

children.text: Only Four Things Can Move the Number
Whatever method a buyer uses, value comes out of four inputs. Every management action worth taking works through at least one of them.

body.caption: The four levers, and who controls them
headers: How it shows up in a valuation

cells: Profit
A higher EBITDA to multiply, or higher cash flows to discount
Pricing, product mix, cost control, capacity utilisation
The multiple, or the discount rate
A higher multiple, or a lower cost of capital, applied to the same profit
Anything that makes future profit more predictable and less risky
Capital tied up
Less working capital and smarter capital expenditure, so more of the profit becomes cash
Supply chain, collections, credit policy, capex discipline
Net debt
What is deducted on the bridge from enterprise value to equity value
Treasury, cash generation and dividend decisions

body.text: Most managers only ever think about the first lever. The second is usually worth as much and is far less contested, because reducing risk costs less than adding profit. Making your earnings believable is a valuation strategy.

children.text: Vellore Instruments Private Limited is a fictional Tamil Nadu maker of industrial sensors. Two years ago it looked like this: revenue ₹250 crore, EBITDA ₹40 crore, one customer contributing 42% of sales, no written long-term contracts, promoter expenses mixed into the accounts, and ₹60 crore of net debt. A buyer would have applied about 8 times EBITDA.

stats.label: Equity value then
stats.context: What the family would have received

children.text: Over two years the management team did four unglamorous things. It exited a low margin product line and repriced two others, taking EBITDA to ₹46 crore. It won three year contracts with its largest customers and brought the top customer down to 25% of sales. It cleaned up the accounts, removing promoter expenses and related-party rent, and closed two years of audits without qualifications. And it released ₹18 crore from receivables and inventory, which went towards repaying debt.

body.caption: Vellore Instruments: where ₹112 crore of equity value came from (₹ crore)

cells: Equity value two years ago
Higher EBITDA, at the old multiple
Re-rating from 8 times to 9 times, on the new EBITDA
Lower net debt from the working capital release
Equity value today

body.title: What created ₹112 crore of equity value

body.text: Read the middle bar again. Moving from 8 times to 9 times added ₹46 crore, almost as much as the entire profit improvement, and it came from contracts, customer spread and clean books rather than from selling a single extra sensor. Equity value rose 43% in two years, and roughly half of that had nothing to do with making more money.

body.title: Isolate the re-rating
body.prompt: Vellore's EBITDA is now ₹46 crore. If the buyer had kept the multiple at 8 times instead of raising it to 9 times, how much lower would enterprise value be, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹46 crore × 1 turn of multiple = ₹46 crore. A single turn of the multiple on a mid-sized business is worth more than most cost-cutting programmes deliver in a year, and it is bought with predictability rather than with effort on the shop floor.

body.title: Profit alone is not enough
body.prompt: Suppose Vellore had improved EBITDA to ₹46 crore and released the working capital, taking net debt to ₹42 crore, but the buyer had refused to move off 8 times because customer concentration was unchanged. What would equity value be, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: (₹46 crore × 8) - ₹42 crore = ₹368 crore - ₹42 crore = ₹326 crore, against ₹372 crore with the re-rating. The same operating performance, ₹46 crore poorer, because one risk was never addressed.

children.text: The Risk Lever, in Plain Terms
A buyer does not lower a multiple because it dislikes you. It lowers the multiple because it is less sure the profit will repeat. Every item below is something a manager can actually change.

body.caption: What raises the multiple a buyer will pay
headers: What you can do about it

cells: One customer is 40% or more of revenue
Lower multiple, price holdbacks, or an escrow
Deliberately grow other accounts, even at lower margin, and get contracts signed
Everything depends on the promoter
Lower multiple and a long lock-in for the seller
Build a second line of management with real authority, and document processes
Revenue is project by project
Lower multiple than a business with repeat or contracted revenue
Convert to annual maintenance contracts, retainers or framework agreements
Accounts carry promoter expenses and related-party dealings
Every number is discounted, and diligence becomes adversarial
Clean them out at least two full financial years before any transaction
Audit qualifications, late filings, open tax disputes
Indemnities, escrow, or a walk-away
Fix compliance hygiene and close disputes where you can
Informal employment and statutory dues
Provisions deducted on the bridge
Regularise contracts, provident fund and gratuity funding
One plant, one location, one supplier
Lower multiple for operational fragility
Second-source critical inputs and document a continuity plan

children.text: The same logic shows up in a discounted cash flow, where it lands on the discount rate instead of the multiple. Take a business generating ₹25 crore of cash flow growing at 5%. At a 14% cost of capital it is worth about ₹277.8 crore. Reduce the rate to 12.5% because the business is visibly less risky, and the same cash flow is worth about ₹333.3 crore, a fifth more.

body.text: The reverse is also true and faster. A single large customer loss, a qualified audit report or a governance incident can take a turn or two off the multiple in a week, long before it shows up in the profit and loss account. Risk builds slowly and reprices instantly.

children.text: Everyday Decisions, Read as Valuation Decisions

body.caption: The same decision, two ways of looking at it

cells: Offering 90 day credit to win a large order
A sales win
Funds the customer for three months, raises working capital, reduces free cash flow
Deferring a machine replacement by a year
Cost saving
Flatters this year's cash flow, and diligence will price the catch-up spending back in
Discounting to hold volume
Defending market share
Permanently resets the margin a buyer capitalises, at the prevailing multiple
Signing a three year contract at a slightly lower price
Leaving money on the table
Buys predictability, which is what a higher multiple is paid for
Hiring a professional CFO or plant head
An overhead
Reduces key person risk, which is a multiple question, not a cost question
Paying rent to a family-owned property company
Normal practice
Becomes a normalisation adjustment and a diligence question
Letting one customer grow to half of revenue
Great customer relationship
The single most common reason mid-sized Indian businesses are marked down

body.title: Which one adds the most value?
body.question: A ₹300 crore revenue components business, valued at 8 times EBITDA of ₹36 crore, is preparing for a sale in two years. Which of these is likely to create the most equity value?
options: A cost reduction programme adding ₹3 crore to EBITDA
Reducing the top customer from 45% to 20% of revenue and signing multi-year contracts, supporting a move from 8 to 9 times
Repaying ₹5 crore of debt from existing cash
Launching a new product line that breaks even in year two
body.explanation: Option A adds ₹3 crore × 8 = ₹24 crore. Option C adds nothing at all: repaying debt with cash reduces both, leaving equity value unchanged. Option D adds nothing yet by definition. Option B adds roughly ₹36 crore, because one turn of multiple applies to the whole ₹36 crore of EBITDA, and it also makes the business easier to sell at all. De-risking is usually the highest return valuation work available to a management team.

body.title: Sequencing the work before a transaction

events.title: Diagnose and clean
events.description: Compute the four levers as they stand today. Separate promoter and personal expenses, document every related-party transaction, and get the last three years of accounts onto a consistent basis.

events.title: Attack the risks that cost you a multiple
events.description: Reduce customer concentration, convert relationships into written contracts, second-source critical inputs, and put a named second line of management in place.

events.title: Fix the economics
events.description: Exit or reprice loss-making lines, improve mix, and release working capital through collections and inventory discipline rather than by stretching suppliers.

events.title: Build the evidence
events.description: Two clean audited years, closed tax positions, regularised employment and statutory dues, and a data room that answers questions before they are asked.

events.title: Go to market
events.description: Run the process with a defensible valuation range, prepared normalisation adjustments, and a story that the numbers support. Nothing material should be fixable at this stage, because it is too late.

body.title: The board wants a number by Friday
body.scenario: You head a business unit at a ₹700 crore revenue family-owned engineering group. The promoters have decided to sell a 30% stake to a private equity fund within a year. At the board meeting, the chairman says the family expects 12 times EBITDA because "that is what the listed players trade at". Your unit's EBITDA is ₹85 crore. Two customers account for 55% of group revenue, the CFO is the chairman's nephew, the group has three open GST disputes, and last year's audit carried an emphasis of matter on related-party balances.
body.prompt: What would you say to the board, and what would you propose for the next twelve months?
body.modelAnswer:
What I would say:
1. Listed multiples are not our multiple. Listed companies are larger, more diversified, audited to a higher standard, liquid and governed publicly. The gap between 12 times and what we will be offered is not a negotiating gap, it is a risk gap, and every item of it is on our own list.
2. Name the deductions honestly. Customer concentration at 55%, an audit emphasis of matter on related-party balances, open tax disputes and a family CFO are exactly the items a fund prices for. Expect a lower multiple, a portion held in escrow, and indemnities.
3. A minority stake attracts its own discount. The fund gets no control, so it will not pay the price a strategic acquirer might.

What I would propose for twelve months:
4. Close or provide for the GST disputes, and get the emphasis of matter resolved in the next audit. These two are the cheapest value creation available, because they cost management attention rather than money.
5. Break the customer concentration deliberately, with a target of no customer above 30%, and convert the two large relationships into multi-year contracts even at a slightly lower price.
6. Professionalise the finance function. A CFO who is not family, or at minimum an independent finance head reporting to the board, changes how every number we present is received.
7. Separate personal and promoter expenses now, so that we have at least one clean financial year before diligence, and prepare the normalisation schedule ourselves rather than letting the buyer construct it.
8. Get our own valuation done, with a range and a sensitivity grid, so the board debates a defensible number rather than an aspiration. Anchoring the family on 12 times will make every real offer feel like an insult and may kill a fair deal.

body.title: The quiet lever
body.textWithBlank: Reducing customer concentration and signing long-term contracts does not raise profit, but it can raise the ___ a buyer applies to that profit.
body.explanation: One turn of multiple on ₹46 crore of EBITDA was worth ₹46 crore in this lesson's example, nearly as much as the entire profit improvement.

body.title: Valuation hygiene, whatever your role
steps: Know your unit's EBITDA, its trend, and what a normalised version looks like
Know the share of revenue from your largest customer, and have a plan if it is above 30%
Convert repeat business into written multi-year contracts wherever the customer will agree
Keep personal, promoter and related-party items out of the company's accounts
Track the cash conversion cycle monthly, and treat a release of working capital as real value creation
Separate maintenance capital expenditure from growth capital expenditure, and never starve the first to flatter cash flow
Close compliance gaps and disputes early, because they become price deductions later
Build a second line of management, and document the processes that currently live in one person's head
Keep a rolling data room: audited accounts, contracts, statutory records, tax positions

body.label: Screener.in: compare your sector's listed players
body.description: Look up three listed companies in your sector and note their operating margin, return on capital and working capital days. Those are the benchmarks a buyer will hold your business against, and the gaps are your value creation agenda.

cards.definition: A decomposition showing how much of a change in value came from profit, from the multiple and from net debt.
A change in the multiple a buyer applies, usually driven by risk rather than by performance.
The share of revenue from the largest customers. Above roughly 30%, buyers start pricing for it.
Dependence on one individual, usually the promoter, for customers, decisions or know-how.
How clean, repeatable and verifiable reported profit is, before any multiple is applied.
The list of adjustments converting reported profit into sustainable profit, better prepared by the seller than by the buyer.
Part of the purchase price held back to cover risks identified in diligence.

points: Only four things move a valuation: profit, the multiple or discount rate, capital tied up, and net debt.
Vellore Instruments added ₹112 crore of equity value in two years: ₹48 crore from profit, ₹46 crore from a single turn of re-rating, and ₹18 crore from releasing working capital.
De-risking is usually the cheapest lever. Contracts, customer spread, clean books and a second line of management cost less than a profit improvement of the same value.
The same effect appears in a DCF as a lower discount rate: 14% to 12.5% raised the value of the same cash flow by about 20%.
Everyday decisions are valuation decisions. Credit terms, deferred capex, discounting and customer concentration all land in the number.
Nothing material can be fixed in the final quarter. Clean books need two full audited years behind them.
Anchoring your board on a listed company multiple is the fastest way to lose a fair deal.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or transaction advice. Vellore Instruments and the engineering group are fictional, and the multiples used are illustrative. Actual multiples and the effect of any management action depend on the sector, the buyer and the evidence available at the time.
